activities.title: Push a counter for each sound
materials: paper with three boxes drawn in a row
a list of words: map, sit, hop, bug, red, fan, pig, mud
parentPrompts: Keep small items like buttons, coins, and seeds out of mouths, and stay close while your child plays.
Say a word slowly, like "map." Ask: "How many sounds do you hear?" Push one counter into a box for each sound: mmm-aaa-p.
Touch each box left to right and say its sound, then sweep your finger under all three boxes and blend the sounds into the word.
Do five more words from your list. Let your child say the word first, then push the sounds. Ask: "Which sound is in the middle?"
Swap roles: you push the sounds (make one mistake on purpose) and your child fixes it.
Check: your child can say each sound separately and blend them back to the word without your help for at least four of the six words.

subject: literacy
title: Short a and short i word builds

activities.title: Build and read short a and short i words
materials: letters needed: a, i, t, p, n, s, m, b, d, g (write one per card)
parentPrompts: Write the letters on cards, with vowels in a different color if you can. Build "sat" and ask your child to read it by saying each sound and then the word.
Change just one card at a time to make a new word: sat, sit, sip, tip, tap, tan, pan, pin. Ask: "What changed? What does the new word say?"
Mix in a few made-up words such as "dap" or "nid." Ask: "Is that a real word? It is okay to read nonsense words; we are practicing sounds."
Have your child write two of the words on paper while saying the sounds.
Check: they read the changed words without guessing from the first letter. If they guess, point back to the vowel card and slow down.

subject: literacy
title: Short o, u, and e word chains

activities.title: Word chains with o, u, e
materials: list: hop, hug, hen, pot, pup, pet, nut, net, not, bed, bud, bad
parentPrompts: Write "hop" and read it together. Then change only the last letter to make "hog," and ask: "What is the new word?" Change the vowel to make "hug."
Make a chain on paper, changing one letter each time: pot, pet, pit, pat. Read the whole chain aloud each time it grows.
Hold up two cards, for example "bed" and "bud." Ask: "Which one means something you sleep in?" Let your child pick and read the word to prove it.
Let your child build a chain for you to read. Cheer for silly words.
Check: they can read six of the listed words by blending sounds and can say which vowel sound is in the middle of each.

activities.title: Find and read tricky words
materials: highlighter tape or small sticky notes
parentPrompts: Write these on cards: the, was, you, said, are, do, have, of. Explain: "Some words are tricky because part of the word does not sound the way we expect. We learn those by heart."
Read each card and have your child say it. For each, point out the tricky part (for example, the "s" in "was" sounds like z).
Open a familiar picture book. Have your child hunt for the tricky words and mark each one with a sticky note.
Play "flash and slap": lay four cards on the table, say a word, and have your child tap the right card.
Check: your child reads at least six of the eight cards quickly (within a couple of seconds). Keep the missed ones for tomorrow's warm-up.

activities.title: Write sentences with capitals and end marks
materials: a picture your child likes (a photo or a drawing)
parentPrompts: Show the picture. Ask your child to say one complete sentence about it, for example "The dog can run."
Say the sentence together and count the words on your fingers. Then have your child write it, leaving a finger space between words.
Check the sentence together with three questions: "Does it start with a capital letter? Did I leave spaces? Does it end with a period (or a ? or !)?"
Write a second sentence. Help with tricky words and let your child spell the others by listening for the sounds.
Check: both sentences start with a capital and end with a mark. Praise the effort, and do not correct every spelling; one or two fixes is plenty.

activities.title: Hundred chart counting
materials: a hundred chart (or draw a 10 by 12 grid of numbers 1 to 120)
parentPrompts: Count aloud together from 1 to 120 while pointing to each number on the chart. If you only have 1 to 100, count the last row on paper.
Pick a starting number such as 47 and say: "Count on from here." Stop at a number you choose and have your child write it.
Play "cover up": cover four numbers with markers. Ask: "Which numbers are hiding?" Your child reads the numbers on each side and names the hidden ones.
Ask: "What do you notice about the numbers in each column?" (The ones digit repeats.)
Check: your child counts to 120 starting from a number you pick below 120, and writes at least three numerals correctly.

activities.title: Count on from the bigger number
materials: a number line to 20, drawn on paper
parentPrompts: Show 6 blocks in a tub and add 2 more. Ask: "How many in all?" Show how to say 6 and then count on: seven, eight.
Explain: "Start with the bigger number in your head and count on." Do 3 + 5: say 5, then count on six, seven, eight.
Use the drawn number line: hop a finger from the start number and say each hop.
Try five problems: 4 + 1, 5 + 2, 7 + 3, 2 + 6, 3 + 4. Let your child choose blocks or the number line.
Check: your child starts with a number and counts on without starting again from one on at least four problems.

activities.title: Break numbers into two parts
materials: a paper with a big circle and two smaller circles below it (a part-whole mat)
parentPrompts: Put 7 counters in the big circle. Ask: "How can we split them into two parts?" Slide some to the left circle and some to the right.
Record the parts: "5 and 2 make 7." Find as many ways to split 7 as you can (6 and 1, 4 and 3).
Try a different number such as 8 or 10. Ask: "What is the pattern?" (One part gets bigger as the other gets smaller.)
Cover one part and ask: "I had 8. Here are 3. How many are hiding?"
Check: your child finds at least three ways to split a number and says an addition sentence for one of them.

activities.title: Act out addition stories
parentPrompts: Tell a short story: "Four ducks were swimming. Three more ducks came. How many ducks now?" Have your child act it out with toys.
Draw the story as quick circles or dots and write 4 + 3 = 7. Explain that the + means "and then some more joined."
Tell two more stories and let your child choose the numbers (keep the total at 10 or less). Include one about putting two groups together, such as "I have 2 red cars and 5 blue cars."
Ask your child to make up a story for you to solve.
Check: your child solves each story with toys or a drawing and can say the sum in a full sentence.

activities.title: Subtract and find the missing part
materials: a cup to hide counters under
parentPrompts: Show 9 counters. Say: "9 birds on a branch. 4 fly away." Have your child take 4 away and count what is left.
Write 9 - 4 = 5 and read it aloud: "Nine take away four is five."
Now the missing-part game: put 8 counters on the table, hide some under the cup, and leave 3 showing. Ask: "How many are under the cup?" Check by lifting it.
Connect it: "3 + ? = 8, and 8 - 3 = 5. They are partners."
Check: your child solves at least three subtraction problems within 10 and finds one hidden amount.

activities.title: Look closely and describe
materials: a few safe objects from your home (a leaf, a spoon, a sponge, a pinecone, a cup of water)
parentPrompts: Explain: "Scientists use their senses to notice things. We have five: sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste. Today we use sight and touch."
Choose one object. Look closely and say three things you see (color, shape, size). Then feel it and say three things about how it feels (smooth, rough, cold).
Have your child draw the object and label two words. Ask: "What is different between this and the next object?"
Repeat with a second object and compare: "How are they alike? How are they different?"
Ask your child to describe an object without naming it while you guess. Check: they use at least two describing words in a full sentence. Safety: only handle safe objects; never taste unknown things.

activities.title: Feel sound vibrations
materials: a small cardboard box or cup
a bowl, plastic wrap, and a few grains of rice
parentPrompts: Pluck a rubber band stretched across a box. Ask: "What do you hear? What do you see?" Notice it wiggles back and forth; that wiggling is called vibrating.
Put your hand lightly on your throat while humming. Ask: "What do you feel?" Stop humming. "What changed?"
Stretch plastic wrap tightly over a bowl and sprinkle on a few grains of rice. Hum or speak loudly near it and watch the rice move. Keep the rice away from your child's mouth.
Hold a ruler over the edge of a table and flick it. Ask: "What happens when it stops moving?"
Ask: "What do we know about how things make sound?" Check: your child says that things shake or vibrate when they make a sound.

activities.title: Use touch and smell to guess
materials: 5 safe household objects (a spoon, a toy block, a cotton ball, a small apple, a sprig of mint or an orange peel)
parentPrompts: Put one object in the bag without your child seeing it. Have your child feel inside without peeking and describe it aloud: "It is smooth. It is hard."
Ask: "What do you think it is? What clue helped?" Reveal it and talk about which senses helped.
Switch roles: your child hides an object, you describe it and they check your guess.
Smell test with eyes closed: orange peel, mint, a dab of cinnamon. Ask: "Does it smell strong or mild? What does it remind you of?" Check for allergies first and do not taste anything.
Record two objects on paper with a drawing and two describing words. Check: your child uses detail words and says which sense they used.

activities.title: Talk about rules and why they help
materials: a board game or card game your family owns
parentPrompts: Start with a game. Play a round of a familiar game but "forget" one rule. Ask: "Was that fair? Why do games need rules?"
Talk about rules at home, in a store, or at a park. Ask: "What is one rule? Who does it help?"
Have your child draw one rule and write a sentence: "We walk inside."
Ask: "What happens when no one follows a rule?" and let your child answer.
Check: your child names two rules and says how each helps people.

activities.title: Make a fair rule together
materials: a pretend problem, e.g., sharing one toy
parentPrompts: Pose a problem: "Two children want the same swing. What could we do?" Let your child suggest solutions.
Decide on a rule that is fair to both, such as taking turns.
Make a poster with one rule, with a picture. Add the reason for the rule.
Practice: role-play the problem while using the rule.
Check: your child explains why the rule is fair and who made it.
